definition: AI transparency means making relevant information about an AI system available and understandable to the people affected by it. In a product interface, this includes what the AI does, what information it uses, its limitations, and what control the user has.
sources: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, Microsoft HAX (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/haxtoolkit/ai-guidelines/)
contentMarkdown:
# AI Transparency

AI transparency means making relevant information about an AI system available and understandable to the people affected by it. In a product interface, this includes what the AI does, what information it uses, its limitations, and what control the user has.

## What should an AI interface make clear?

Disclose information where it helps a person understand or influence the task.

| User question | Useful information |
|---|---|
| What is happening? | Whether AI is drafting, recommending, or taking action |
| What is this based on? | Relevant records, documents, or other inputs |
| What might be wrong? | Task-specific limitations and missing information |
| Can I change it? | Editing, correction, cancellation, and review options |
| What has happened already? | Completed actions, failures, and uncertain outcomes |

An “AI-powered” badge identifies a technology. It does not answer these questions by itself.

## Example: drafting a support reply

Suppose an assistant drafts a reply using a customer message and a booking record. The interface identifies it as a draft, shows the relevant source details, and makes clear that it has not been sent.

The reviewer can edit the text and check the conditions behind any proposed statement. If the assistant cannot retrieve the booking, the interface exposes that gap instead of presenting a complete-looking answer based on assumed details.

After sending, the product reports the actual result. A draft and a successfully delivered message are different states.

## Transparency vs. explainability

Transparency covers the system's role, inputs, boundaries, and operation. [Explainable AI](/glossary/explainable-ai.html) focuses on making behavior or results understandable.

A product may clearly disclose that a model generated an answer without being able to explain the result faithfully. It should represent both facts accurately.

Transparency also does not require showing every technical detail. Select information for the audience and decision, with access to further detail when useful.

## How do you test transparency?

Ask people to explain what the system has done, what it can do next, and which parts they can control. Test these questions during real tasks, including missing information and failures.

Watch for misleading labels and default states. A prominent “Verified” label needs a defined verification process and scope. Clearer wording is preferable to a reassuring claim the product cannot substantiate.

## Related terms

contentMarkdown:
# AI in UX Research

AI in UX research is the use of AI tools to support research activities such as preparing questions, organizing observations, or drafting summaries. Generated material must remain distinguishable from evidence collected from participants and actual product use.

## Where can AI support UX research?

A tool can propose interview questions, organize supplied notes, suggest candidate themes, or help locate relevant passages. Each use still needs a clear research question and a way to check the result.

| Activity | Useful support | Required check |
|---|---|---|
| Preparation | Draft questions or task wording | Remove leading assumptions |
| Transcription | Produce a searchable draft | Verify important words and speaker attribution |
| Analysis | Suggest clusters or exceptions | Compare with the original observations |
| Reporting | Draft a concise account | Trace claims and quotes to evidence |

An AI-generated persona or hypothetical answer is an assumption to investigate. It does not establish what a real participant thinks or does.

## Example: checking a proposed research theme

Suppose a researcher supplies approved, de-identified notes about a quote-request form. A tool proposes a theme: “People avoid sharing a phone number.”

The researcher checks the underlying sessions. Some participants may object to calls; others may not understand why the field is required. Combining these into one explanation could lead to the wrong design response.

Keep the observations, interpretation, and proposed action separate. Preserve contradictory evidence and the boundaries of the study.

## How do you preserve traceability?

Give observations stable references to sessions, passages, or timestamps. Ask for those references in generated summaries, then verify that they exist and support the claim.

Do not turn a paraphrase into a quotation. Check any quote against the original recording or transcript. Report sample counts only when the underlying records and counting rule support them.

GOV.UK's analysis guidance distinguishes observed evidence from its interpretation and resulting actions. AI support should preserve that distinction.

## What about participant data?

Use an approved workflow for the actual data involved. Check consent, access, retention, and the tool's handling of uploaded material before submitting recordings or notes.

Removing a name does not necessarily remove identifying details from a story. Supply only what the task needs, and keep human review of consequential interpretations.

Evaluate the workflow by the quality and usefulness of the findings, including checking effort. A faster summary that loses important exceptions can make the research less useful.

## Related terms

- [Synthetic User Testing](/glossary/synthetic-user-testing.html)
- [ResearchOps](/glossary/researchops.html)
- [AI-assisted Design](/glossary/ai-assisted-design.html)
- [Product Discovery](/glossary/product-discovery.html)

name: Context Window
definition: A context window is the amount of information a language model can process within a request or interaction, usually measured in tokens. It limits the instructions, conversation, retrieved material, and other content available when the model generates a response.
sources: Effective context engineering for AI agents, Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)
contentMarkdown:
# Context Window

A context window is the amount of information a language model can process within a request or interaction, usually measured in tokens. It limits the instructions, conversation, retrieved material, and other content available when the model generates a response.

## What counts toward the context window?

Depending on the model and API, context can include system instructions, user messages, conversation history, tool definitions, tool results, documents, and generated output. Multimodal inputs also consume capacity under provider-specific rules.

Input, output, and reasoning budgets are not identical across providers. Check the selected model's documentation before planning around a particular limit.

A token is a unit used by the model, not a fixed number of English words. File size and page count are also unreliable substitutes for the actual token budget.

## Context window vs. training vs. memory

| Concept | What it describes |
|---|---|
| Training | The process that produces the model's learned parameters |
| Context window | Information available within the current processing budget |
| Product memory | Application features that store and later supply selected information |

A saved conversation is not necessarily supplied in full on every request. A memory feature may retrieve a small relevant part of stored information. Neither means the model has unlimited access to every previous interaction.

## Example: a long policy conversation

A support tool starts with a policy document, a customer message, and booking details. Later turns add search results and corrections.

As the conversation grows, the application may need to retrieve relevant passages, summarize earlier material, or ask for a missing detail. The exact overflow behavior depends on implementation; a request might be rejected, shortened, or processed through a context-management mechanism.

If summarization drops an important exception, the interface should make the relevant source available again rather than asking the user to trust a compressed account.

## Why doesn't more context guarantee a better answer?

A larger window allows more information to fit. It does not establish that the information is relevant, accurate, or used reliably.

[Context engineering](/glossary/context-engineering.html) concerns selecting and maintaining useful information within that budget. Test long interactions as well as short prompts, especially when earlier decisions or corrections matter.

Expose context limitations when they affect the task. Users need a recovery path when the system no longer has the information required to continue accurately.

## Related terms

- [Context Engineering](/glossary/context-engineering.html)
- [Context Drift](/glossary/context-drift.html)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](/glossary/retrieval-augmented-generation-rag.html)
- [AI Grounding](/glossary/ai-grounding.html)

- [Effective context engineering for AI agents, Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)

name: Explainable AI
definition: Explainable AI (XAI) refers to methods and practices that make an AI system's behavior or results understandable to people. In product design, an explanation should help a specific audience assess an output or decide what to do next.
sources: Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence, NIST (https://www.nist.gov/publications/four-principles-explainable-artificial-intelligence)
contentMarkdown:
# Explainable AI

Explainable AI (XAI) refers to methods and practices that make an AI system's behavior or results understandable to people. In product design, an explanation should help a specific audience assess an output or decide what to do next.

## What makes an explanation useful?

Different people need different explanations. A person reviewing a recommendation may need the relevant evidence and limitations. A developer investigating a failure may need model diagnostics.

NIST describes four principles: provide an explanation, make it meaningful to the intended audience, represent the system's process accurately, and recognize its knowledge limits. These are principles for explanation quality, not a requirement to display every internal detail.

## Example: explaining an expense flag

Suppose an assistant flags an expense for review. The reviewer needs to know which submitted values and policy provisions support that flag, what information is missing, and how to correct or challenge it.

“AI detected a problem” does not support that decision. A concise explanation connecting a particular date or amount to a relevant policy passage may help.

If the product cannot establish that the cited factor caused the model's result, it should avoid presenting that factor as a verified causal explanation. Showing relevant evidence and explaining the limitation may be more accurate.

## Explanation vs. generated rationale

A language model can produce a convincing account of why an answer seems reasonable. That account is not automatically a faithful record of the computation that produced it.

Distinguish evidence, system rules, model interpretation methods, and generated summaries. Do not imply that a conversational explanation exposes the model's complete reasoning.

Likewise, an explanation does not establish that the outcome is correct or fair. Those questions require their own evaluation.

## How should designers choose the level of detail?

Identify the decision, audience, and consequences. Present the most useful information at the point where it is needed, with a route to supporting detail.

Test whether people understand the explanation and use it appropriately. More text or a confidence badge may create reassurance without improving judgment.

Give users a next step: inspect a source, edit an input, request review, or decline the recommendation. The explanation is useful when it supports informed action, not merely when it sounds plausible.

## Related terms

- [AI Transparency](/glossary/ai-transparency.html)
- [Trust Calibration in AI](/glossary/trust-calibration-ai.html)
- [AI Grounding](/glossary/ai-grounding.html)
- [Human-in-the-Loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop-hitl.html)

- [Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence, NIST](https://www.nist.gov/publications/four-principles-explainable-artificial-intelligence)
- [Explainability and Trust, Google PAIR](https://pair.withgoogle.com/chapter/explainability-trust/)

name: Prompt Injection
definition: Prompt injection is an attack that puts instructions into content an AI system processes, attempting to redirect its behavior beyond the intended task. The instructions may come from a direct user input or from an external source such as a document or web page.
sources: Prompt Injection, OWASP Gen AI Security Project (https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)
contentMarkdown:
# Prompt Injection

Prompt injection is an attack that puts instructions into content an AI system processes, attempting to redirect its behavior beyond the intended task. The instructions may come from a direct user input or from an external source such as a document or web page.

## Direct vs. indirect prompt injection

A direct injection is supplied through an input to the AI system. An indirect injection arrives through material the system reads while performing another task.

For example, an agent may need to summarize an uploaded document. An instruction embedded in that document can try to make the agent perform an unrelated action. The document is task data; it should not receive the authority of the person who delegated the task.

Prompt injection differs from a hallucination. The central issue is influence over instructions and actions, rather than unsupported generated facts.

## Example: a supplier document in an operations tool

Suppose an assistant reads a supplier's attachment to extract booking details. The attachment also contains instructions to send internal records elsewhere.

A well-designed workflow does not let a document grant new permissions. The application limits which records the assistant can access and which destinations it can use. If a consequential action needs review, the interface shows its actual target, content, and effect.

A confirmation labeled only “Continue?” gives the reviewer little basis for detecting an unintended action.

## What belongs in the product design?

Make permissions and action boundaries understandable. Separate reading a source, preparing a change, and committing that change when their consequences differ.

For consequential operations, provide a review that lets the person inspect the proposed action. Show what completed, what failed, and whether anything may already have changed. Recovery needs to account for partial execution.

The appropriate controls depend on the operation. Requiring confirmation for every harmless step can obscure the decisions that actually need attention.

## Why are system prompts insufficient?

Instructions asking a model to ignore malicious content can be one layer, but they are not a complete security boundary. Access checks, authorization, constrained tools, and output handling must be enforced by the application.

OWASP recommends measures including least-privilege access, separation of external content, and human review for high-risk actions. Test the complete workflow against adversarial inputs as well as ordinary tasks.

Treat a strong-looking refusal or successful demonstration as one observation, not evidence that all prompt injection has been prevented.

## Related terms

- [Tool Calling](/glossary/tool-calling-function-calling.html)
- [Agentic UX](/glossary/agentic-ux.html)
- [Human-in-the-Loop](/glossary/human-in-the-loop-hitl.html)
